title: Classify an Address String
statement:
A form field accepts a network address. Given the raw string text, return "IPv4" if it is a valid IPv4 address, "IPv6" if it is a valid IPv6 address, and "Neither" otherwise.

  • IPv4: exactly four parts separated by .. Each part is a decimal number from 0 to 255, written with 1 to 3 digits and no leading zero: "0" is fine, "07" and "00" are not.
  • IPv6: exactly eight groups separated by :. Each group has 1 to 4 hexadecimal digits (0–9, a–f, A–F). Leading zeros are allowed here. The :: shorthand is not: every group must be written out.

examples.why: Four parts, each between 0 and 255, and the lone 0 is allowed.
Eight groups of 1 to 4 hex digits. The leading zero in 0204 and the capital F are both allowed.
The part 01 has a leading zero, which IPv4 forbids even though its value is in range.

constraints: text contains only English letters, digits, '.' and ':'
hints: Decide which format to try by the separator the text contains, then check the pieces one by one.
Splitting on the separator keeps empty pieces, which catches leading, trailing and doubled separators for free. Check the piece count first.
For IPv4 check, in this order: length 1 to 3, all digits, no leading zero unless the piece is exactly "0", value at most 255. For IPv6: length 1 to 4, all hex digits.

explain.intuition:
This is a careful-reading problem, like writing a form validator. There is no clever trick: the job is to list every rule and check each piece against all of them, without letting a forgiving built-in parser accept something it should not.

Split on . or : and keep empty pieces, so "1..1.1" and "1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8:" fail on the piece check. Do not use parseInt to test digits: parseInt("1e1") is 1, and it ignores trailing junk. Check the characters yourself, then convert.
steps: If text contains a ., split on it. It must give 4 pieces.
Each IPv4 piece: 1 to 3 characters, all digits, no leading 0 when longer than one character, value ≤ 255. Pass all four and return "IPv4".
Else if text contains a :, split on it. It must give 8 pieces, each 1 to 4 hex digits. Then return "IPv6".
pitfalls: Using parseInt or Number to decide whether a piece is numeric. Both accept strings the rules reject.
Applying the no-leading-zero rule to IPv6. There, 0db8 is valid.
Checking only the value of an IPv4 piece and not its length: "0001" or a very long piece must fail before conversion.

solutions.title: Split and check each piece
solutions.idea: Split on the separator, check the piece count, then validate every piece's length and characters by hand.

solutions.title: Whole-string patterns
solutions.idea: Spell each format as an anchored pattern. The IPv4 piece pattern lists the allowed ranges: 250–255, 200–249, 100–199, 10–99 and 0–9.

followups: Support the IPv6 :: shorthand, which stands for one or more groups of zeros and may appear at most once.
Return the address in a canonical form (for IPv6, lowercase with leading zeros dropped). What new edge cases appear?
